2.5 Monetary Policy

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

Goals

Section titled “Goals”

The central bank of the United States is the Federal Reserve System (the Fed). Congress has given it two goals (the dual mandate): maximum employment and stable prices (plus moderate long-term interest rates). The Fed defines stable prices as 2% inflation measured by the PCE price index (2.1 Macroeconomic Data, since 2012); it revised its statement of longer-run goals in August 2025, keeping the 2% target.

Interest rate policy is decided by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which meets 8 times a year. The central bank’s decisions are independent of the government: the temptation to cut rates before an election for a temporary boom would damage inflation expectations, and 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations showed why expectations matter.

The model of 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations tells us what monetary policy can do: in the short run, by changing interest rates it moves aggregate demand, narrowing the output gap and stabilizing inflation; in the long run it determines inflation but cannot keep output above its potential.

Tools

Section titled “Tools”

What the FOMC sets is a target range for the federal funds rate: the rate at which banks lend reserves to each other overnight. On October 28, 2026 the FOMC kept the target range at 3.75%–4.00% (Federal Reserve, October 28, 2026).

How does the Fed keep market rates inside this range? 2.3 Money and Banking said that since 2008 banks have held large reserves; the Fed now runs an “ample reserves” framework that relies mainly on two rates:

  • Interest on reserve balances (IORB): the rate banks earn on money held at the Fed, currently 3.90%. A bank that can earn 3.90% risk-free from the Fed will not lend to others at a much lower rate.
  • The overnight reverse repo rate (ON RRP): institutions such as money market funds, which cannot hold reserve accounts at the Fed, can lend to the Fed and earn 3.75%; this puts a floor under market rates.

In addition, banks can borrow from the Fed’s discount window, currently at 4.0%, which limits how high market rates go (all rates effective October 29, 2026, Fed implementation note). When the FOMC wants to raise rates by 0.25 percentage points, it raises all of these rates by 0.25 percentage points.

Rates cannot go too low: if bank deposits paid clearly negative rates, people would hold cash instead. Nominal rates cannot go far below zero; this is called the zero lower bound. In 2008–2015 and 2020–2022 the US federal funds rate was near zero. The central bank then has two more tools:

  • Quantitative easing (QE): buying large amounts of long-term Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities to push long-term rates down directly. The Fed’s assets reached about 9 trillion dollars in 2022 (Federal Reserve H.4.1 release). The reverse, reducing bond holdings, is called quantitative tightening (QT).
  • Forward guidance: stating what future rates will be, which affects expectations of future short rates and therefore today’s long rates (Exercises Question 5).
Check C1
The interest rate on reserve balances is 3.90% and the overnight reverse repo rate 3.75%. Would a bank with ample reserves lend them overnight to another bank at 3.5%?
Do reserves held at the Fed earn interest? At what rate?
Even if the borrower were riskless, which is higher: 3.5% or what the Fed pays?
The federal funds market is itself a market where banks lend reserves to each other. Why, then, would this bank refuse?

The Taylor rule

Section titled “The Taylor rule”

How high should the central bank set its rate? The economist John Taylor (1993) proposed a simple rule called the Taylor rule:

i=r∗+π+0.5 (π−πT)+0.5 gapi = r^* + \pi + 0.5\,(\pi - \pi^T) + 0.5\,\text{gap}i=r∗+π+0.5(π−πT)+0.5gap

where iii is the nominal policy rate, π\piπ is inflation over the past year, πT=2%\pi^T = 2\%πT=2% is the target and gap\text{gap}gap is the output gap (%). r∗r^*r∗ is called the neutral interest rate: the real interest rate that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. When inflation equals the target and the output gap is zero, the nominal rate equals r∗+πr^* + \pir∗+π and the real rate equals r∗r^*r∗.

The rule has two main points:

  • For each point that inflation is higher, the nominal rate rises 1.5 points, more than 1 point. Then the real rate also rises, which is needed to restrain demand (the Taylor principle).
  • r∗r^*r∗ cannot be observed directly, only estimated, and estimates differ considerably. The rule’s answer is sensitive to r∗r^*r∗ and to the inflation measure used.

So the Taylor rule is not a formula the central bank must obey but a reference: when the actual rate departs clearly from the rule, there should be a reason.

Check C2
In Figure 3-1, keep inflation and the neutral rate fixed and move the output gap from 0 to −2% (a recession). The rule's recommended nominal rate:
What is the coefficient on the output gap in the rule?
With output below potential, does the central bank want to stimulate or restrain demand? Should the rate rise or fall?
In the Taylor rule, does the rate respond only to inflation?

Transmission

Section titled “Transmission”

The federal funds rate is only an overnight rate. How does it affect the economy?

  • Other interest rates: changes in short rates, and in expected future short rates, pass through to Treasury yields, mortgage rates and business loan rates.
  • Asset prices: when rates rise, the present value of future cash flows falls (present value), stock and real estate prices fall, household wealth falls, and consumption falls with it.
  • The exchange rate: higher rates attract foreign money, the currency appreciates, and exports fall (2.7 The Open Economy).
  • Credit: when rates rise, borrowers’ collateral loses value and debt payments rise, and banks lend more cautiously.
  • Expectations: the central bank’s actions and statements change expectations of inflation and future policy, which affect how wages and prices are set.

All of these channels take time. Monetary policy generally affects output after about a year and inflation later still, and the lags vary (“long and variable lags”). So the central bank must decide on the basis of forecasts; it cannot wait until inflation has already come down before it stops raising rates.

Check C3
A rate hike raises the return investors require on every asset by 1 percentage point, with expected cash flows unchanged. Which asset's price falls by the largest percentage?
Does this stock's value come mostly from near or distant cash flows? Are near cash flows discounted over many periods?
All its cash comes back in a year. How much does its price change when the discount rate rises 1 percentage point?
Does the effect of a change in the discount rate on present value depend on the number of periods discounted?

How markets see the central bank

Section titled “How markets see the central bank”

As with the data releases of 2.1 Macroeconomic Data, markets react to the central bank’s decision according to how it differs from expectations. Before an FOMC meeting, investors have already formed expectations from prices such as federal funds futures. A rate cut that was expected hardly moves markets; a surprise decision to hold, even though rates “did not change”, raises bond yields and lowers stock prices.

So investors care not only about the rate decision itself but also about the FOMC statement, the Chair’s press conference and the members’ projections of future rates: these change expectations of the whole future path of rates.

Check C4
The FOMC decides to leave rates unchanged, so short-term Treasury yields and stock prices will not move much that day.
What did market prices already reflect before the meeting? What if the market had expected a cut?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • The Fed’s dual mandate is maximum employment and stable prices; the inflation target is 2% PCE inflation.
  • The FOMC sets a target range for the federal funds rate (3.75%–4.00% in October 2026) and keeps market rates in the range with the rate on reserves, the ON RRP rate and the discount rate.
  • Nominal rates have a zero lower bound; then quantitative easing and forward guidance can be used.
  • Taylor rule: i=r∗+π+0.5(π−πT)+0.5 gapi = r^* + \pi + 0.5(\pi - \pi^T) + 0.5\,\text{gap}i=r∗+π+0.5(π−πT)+0.5gap. When inflation rises, the nominal rate must rise by more, so that the real rate rises; estimates of the neutral rate are uncertain.
  • Monetary policy affects the economy through other interest rates, asset prices, the exchange rate, credit and expectations, with long and variable lags.
  • Markets react to the central bank’s decisions according to how they differ from expectations.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1 ★
In September 2026, the US core PCE price index was up 3.1% from a year earlier and the PCE price index 3.6% (BEA, October 29, 2026). October unemployment was 4.1% and the CBO's natural rate about 4.4%, so by Okun's law the output gap is about +0.6%.
(a) With r∗=1%r^* = 1\%r∗=1% and core PCE inflation, what rate does the Taylor rule suggest? With PCE inflation instead?
(b) Compare with the target range of 3.75%–4.00% at the time. Do these numbers show that the Fed's rate is "wrong"? Name at least two factors the rule cannot take into account.
Question 2
Suppose a central bank sets i=r∗+2+0.8(π−2)i = r^* + 2 + 0.8(\pi - 2)i=r∗+2+0.8(π−2) (r∗=1%r^* = 1\%r∗=1%, ignoring the output gap).
(a) If inflation rises from 2% to 4%, by how much do the nominal and real rates change?
(b) Using aggregate demand from 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations, explain whether such a central bank makes inflation tend to stabilize or keep rising.
Question 3
In a severe recession, inflation is 0.5%, the output gap is −5%, and the neutral rate is estimated at 0.5%.
(a) What rate does the Taylor rule suggest?
(b) Can the central bank deliver it? If not, what other tools can it use, and how does each affect the economy?
Question 4 ★
For a 400,000-dollar, 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, a rise in the rate from 6% to 7% raises the monthly payment from about 2,398 to about 2,661 dollars (about 11%).
(a) Most US mortgages are 30-year fixed-rate loans. After a rate hike, how do households that already have a mortgage and households buying now differ in how they are affected? How does this affect the speed of monetary policy transmission?
(b) Homeowners who have locked in a low rate must borrow again at the new, higher rate if they move. What does this do to the supply of existing homes for sale?
Question 5
Suppose the 2-year rate is about the average of this year's 1-year rate and the 1-year rate expected next year (ignoring risk compensation). This year's 1-year rate is 4%, and markets expected it to stay at 4% next year.
(a) The central bank leaves rates unchanged today but announces that it will probably cut to 3% next year, and markets believe it. How does the 2-year rate change?
(b) What does this show about how forward guidance affects the economy without changing today's rate? What does it require to work?
